clue.text: Lock for one sentenced to play with elliptical billiards balls ?

definitions.text: Lock for one sentenced to play with elliptical billiards balls ?

parts.words: Lock for one sentenced to play with elliptical billiards balls ?
parts.note: a lock of hair is a curl; in The Mikado the billiard sharp is sentenced to play 'with a twisted cue and elliptical billiard balls', so his cue is a curly one

explanation.surface: A gaoler muses on a prisoner condemned to a farcical game of billiards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lock' looks like a prison lock; it is a lock of hair. The Mikado's punishment for the billiard sharp is a twisted cue, which said quickly is the fancy flourish the answer names.
explanation.definitionFit: A fancy twisting curl, in hair or in handwriting, is the ornamental flourish meant, and the Mikado's twisted cue sounds the same.

clue.text: Heads buttered up over tea

definitions.meaning: crumpet is old slang for the head
the griddle cakes served toasted and buttered at teatime

explanation.surface: Bosses are flattered at an afternoon tea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Buttered up' looks like flattery; it is literal butter on the British teatime griddle cakes. 'Crumpet' is also old slang for the head.
explanation.definitionFit: Old slang calls the head a crumpet, and the spongy griddle cakes are toasted and buttered at teatime.

clue.text: Hammer and sickle? No, duster

parts.note: the Soviet emblem sits on a red flag, but the red flag meant is the British merchant navy's, nicknamed the red duster

explanation.surface: Someone corrects a guess about tools to a cleaning cloth.
explanation.walkthrough: The Soviet hammer and sickle flies on red, but the flag meant is the British merchant navy's, called the 'Red Duster'.
explanation.definitionFit: The British merchant ship's flag is red with the Union flag in its corner, a naval banner nicknamed the red duster.

clue.text: I would almost risk taking the chair up in Wales

parts.note: I'd is the contraction of I would

indicators.note: almost the whole word risk, its final letter left off

explanation.surface: Someone nearly dares to take the chair at a Welsh meeting.
explanation.walkthrough: Cader Idris, a Welsh mountain, means the chair of Idris, the legendary giant. 'Almost' cuts the K from 'risk'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Welsh peak Cader Idris is named as the seat of Idris, a giant of legend.

clue.text: More ideal

parts.note: read as an adjective comparing perfection, or as the perfect state imagined by Sir Thomas More

explanation.surface: Something is even more perfect.
explanation.walkthrough: 'More' looks like a comparative; it is Sir Thomas More, author of Utopia.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Thomas More's imagined perfect island gave its name to visionary idealism.

clue.text: Psychedelic experience old style students work for

parts.note: a drug-induced hallucinatory episode is a trip
OS is the standard abbreviation for Old Style, the calendar dating before 1752

explanation.surface: An acid trip and old-fashioned undergraduates hint at drugs and dons.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the honours examination at Cambridge University, which undergraduates work towards.
explanation.definitionFit: Cambridge honours degrees are awarded by examination in a subject's parts, the goal undergraduates labour towards.

clue.text: Banish as in "As You Like It

definitions.meaning: to send a student down from university for a time
the play's exiled duke and courtiers live a country life in the Forest of Arden

explanation.surface: A theatre note about exile in Shakespeare's comedy.
explanation.walkthrough: The first sense is the university one, sending a student away from college for a while; the second is to go and live in the countryside, as the courtiers do in Arden.
explanation.definitionFit: Universities send students down temporarily, and to live as country folk is a rural existence, both covered by the verb.

clue.text: .The Gunner's mascot of ancient build

definitions.meaning: a dog of that name served as a mascot
the ancient city in Jordan carved out of rock

explanation.surface: An artillery regiment's mascot is very old.
explanation.walkthrough: The ancient city in Jordan is cut into rose-red sandstone cliffs.
explanation.definitionFit: A dog of that name was a mascot, and the Nabataean city in Jordan was hewn from rock in antiquity.

clue.text: " The whitewashed wall, the nicely —— floor " (Goldsmith)

definitions.text: " The whitewashed wall, the nicely —— floor " (Goldsmith)

parts.words: " The whitewashed wall, the nicely —— floor " (Goldsmith)
parts.note: a gap to fill from a line of Oliver Goldsmith's poem The Deserted Village, describing the village inn

explanation.surface: A quotation describing a tidy country room.
explanation.walkthrough: Fill the blank from Goldsmith's The Deserted Village; floors were strewn with sand to keep them clean.
explanation.definitionFit: Inn floors were strewn with fine grit to keep them clean, as Goldsmith's line says.

clue.text: Runny honey, Edward

parts.note: mel is the Latin word for honey, used in pharmacy
Ted is a pet form of Edward

explanation.surface: Edward's honey has gone liquid.
explanation.walkthrough: MEL is Latin for honey, a crossword favourite.
explanation.definitionFit: Butter or ice that has turned liquid in the heat has thawed into a runny state.

clue.text: Rare as a Shakespearian bawd was not

definitions.meaning: rare meat is lightly cooked, not fully done

definitions.text: as a Shakespearian bawd was not
definitions.meaning: Mistress Overdone is the bawd in Measure for Measure, so she was the opposite

explanation.surface: A rare remark about a brothel-keeper in Shakespeare.
explanation.walkthrough: Mistress Overdone keeps the brothel in Shakespeare's Measure for Measure; the answer is the opposite of her name.
explanation.definitionFit: Steak served rare is lightly cooked, and the opposite of Overdone names the bawd's contrary.

clue.text: Suppressed by the session

definitions.meaning: to squash or silence something is to crush it underfoot or by sitting
a committee or court in session sits on a case it is considering

explanation.surface: A committee meeting silences someone.
explanation.definitionFit: To quash a proposal is to squash it flat, and a court in session considers, or sits over, the cases before it.

clue.text: Linen of the long-distance runner ?

definitions.meaning: linen here is underclothing, the drawers worn under trousers
a distance runner breathes hard and gasps

explanation.surface: Asking what kit a marathon runner wears.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Linen' means underwear, the old sense of body linen; the runner's question mark points to the verb, gasping for breath.
explanation.definitionFit: Underclothing is drawers, and an exhausted athlete gasps for breath, both the same word.

clue.text: To dismantle one tin crate is far from simple

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I

indicators.note: taking a crate apart and rebuilding it means rearranging these letters

explanation.surface: Taking apart a tin crate turns out to be a fiddly job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To dismantle' rearranges I (one) and TINCRATE to make the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Something involved and full of detail is complicated, the opposite of simple.

clue.text: A hero given the loving-cup

parts.note: the Arthurian knight who drank a love potion with Isolde, binding them in fatal love

explanation.surface: A champion is presented with a trophy cup.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Loving-cup' looks like a sports trophy; here it is the love potion the Cornish knight shares with Isolde.
explanation.definitionFit: The legendary knight of Cornwall fell in love with Isolde after they drank a love potion together.

clue.text: Old Weller at the piano, accompanied by the handyman in " The Land of my Fathers "

definitions.text: in " The Land of my Fathers "

parts.note: Tony Weller is Sam Weller's father in Dickens's Pickwick Papers
p is the musical abbreviation for piano, softly
Handy Andy is the proverbial odd-job man

explanation.surface: An old man playing piano duets with a handyman in a Welsh song.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Land of my Fathers' is the Welsh national anthem, so the definition is a place in Wales: a Rhondda town.
explanation.definitionFit: The Rhondda mining town lies in Wales, the country the Welsh anthem calls Land of my Fathers.

clue.text: Small size seven took a fair domestic

definitions.meaning: people of very small stature
the seven little men of the fairy tale took in Snow White, who kept house for them

explanation.surface: Seven small people hire a pretty housemaid.
explanation.walkthrough: Snow White, the 'fair domestic', kept house for the seven little men of the story.
explanation.definitionFit: Undersized people are little folk, and the fairy tale's seven little miners sheltered Snow White as their housekeeper.

clue.text: Déclassé stamp, shortly

definitions.meaning: cheap and lowly, worth only a few old pence
a postage stamp worth four old pence, named by its value with the word stamp left off for short

explanation.surface: A postage stamp of no social standing.
explanation.walkthrough: In old British money a coin or stamp worth four pence was cheap; 'shortly' says the word stamp is left off.
explanation.definitionFit: Something worth four old pence is cheap and common, and a postage stamp of that value goes by the same short name.

clue.text: He is repellent

parts.note: read as he is disgusting, but meaning he repels attacks

explanation.surface: Someone is described as revolting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Repellent' looks like disgusting; here it is one who repels attackers.
explanation.definitionFit: One who repels an attack protects a position or a goal.

clue.text: A denial to the corporal by an unknown man

parts.note: no is a word of denial
Corporal Nym is a rogue in Shakespeare's Henry V and The Merry Wives of Windsor

explanation.surface: Someone unidentified refuses a request from a corporal.
explanation.walkthrough: The corporal is Shakespeare's Nym, a companion of Falstaff and Pistol.
explanation.definitionFit: A person whose name is withheld, or a pseudonym, is nameless and so unknown.

clue.text: I drink heavily, do I—even monumentally ?

parts.note: the speaker's I becomes me
to tope is to drink alcohol to excess

explanation.surface: A drinker asks whether he drinks on a monumental scale.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a panel between the triglyphs of a Doric frieze, part of monumental architecture.
explanation.definitionFit: In a Doric temple frieze the square panels between the triglyphs are part of the building's monumental decoration.

clue.text: Take it as Stanley did

definitions.meaning: to take it that something is so is to assume it
the explorer Henry Morton Stanley greeted David Livingstone with 'Dr Livingstone

explanation.surface: Accepting something the way an explorer once did.
explanation.walkthrough: Stanley's famous greeting on finding Livingstone in Africa used the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To take something for granted is to assume it, and Stanley's famous greeting used that very verb.

clue.text: Apparition that delighted Wordsworth

definitions.meaning: a ghost or spectre
Wordsworth's poem begins 'She was a ... of delight'

explanation.surface: Wordsworth is pleased by a vision.
explanation.walkthrough: Wordsworth's poem opens 'She was a Phantom of delight'.
explanation.definitionFit: A ghostly spectre is a spirit seen, and Wordsworth called his wife a spectre of delight.

clue.text: One of those scholarly debt-collector's north of the Tweed ?

definitions.text: One of those scholarly debt-collector's north of the Tweed ?

parts.words: One of those scholarly debt-collector's north of the Tweed ?
parts.note: duns are debt collectors, Duns is a Scottish town

explanation.surface: A Scottish bailiff with a learned streak.
explanation.walkthrough: John Duns Scotus was a medieval philosopher; a dun is a debt-collector, and Duns is a town north of the River Tweed in Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: The medieval philosopher John Duns surname is the Latin for a Scot, the second part of the schoolman's name.

clue.text: Lovely, needlewoman

definitions.meaning: a lovely is a beautiful woman, and the Egyptian queen is the type of beauty
the London obelisk on the Embankment is called her Needle

explanation.surface: A pretty seamstress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Needlewoman' suggests sewing, but the needle is the ancient Egyptian obelisk on London's Thames Embankment that bears her name.
explanation.definitionFit: The Egyptian queen is the classic beauty, and a London obelisk is called her Needle.

clue.text: Laud

parts.note: to praise highly, not the archbishop of that name

explanation.surface: A single word of praise.
explanation.definitionFit: To praise lavishly is to glorify.

clue.text: One Tucker performed for more than this composer

indicators.note: what Tucker sang for is longer than the composer's name by one letter, so a letter is dropped from it

parts.note: in the nursery rhyme little Tommy Tucker sings for his supper

explanation.surface: A singer called Tucker did more than this composer for his meal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Little Tommy Tucker sings for his supper'; that word is more than the answer by its last R. Franz von Suppé wrote the Light Cavalry overture.
explanation.definitionFit: Franz von Suppé was the Austrian writer of operettas and overtures such as Light Cavalry.

clue.text: Tread softly, there's a broken slate

indicators.note: a broken slate is in pieces, so its letters are reassembled

explanation.surface: A warning to step lightly near a cracked roof slate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broken' rearranges SLATE.
explanation.definitionFit: To creep silently is to move by stealth.

clue.text: Gould takes it-back to Mr. Big

indicators.note: the whole run of name and pronoun is read backwards

parts.note: Nat Gould was a popular writer of horse-racing novels

explanation.surface: A man named Gould returns something to a gang boss.
explanation.walkthrough: Nat Gould wrote horse-racing novels in their hundreds; 'back' reads his first name and the clue's own 'it' in reverse as one run.
explanation.definitionFit: A giant of Greek myth, and so any colossal figure or bigwig.

clue.text: It's modelled with a decorative design

definitions.text: It's modelled with a decorative design

parts.words: It's modelled with a decorative design
parts.note: something modelled on a template and bearing repeated ornament

explanation.surface: A model wears something with a decorative motif.
explanation.definitionFit: Cloth bearing repeated ornament, made to a template or model, is decorated with a design.

clue.text: Bishop's College

parts.note: a Cambridge college founded in memory of George Augustus ..., Bishop of New Zealand and Lichfield

explanation.surface: A college run by the church.
explanation.walkthrough: The Cambridge college is named after the Victorian bishop George Augustus Selwyn.
explanation.definitionFit: The Cambridge college bears the surname of the bishop it commemorates.

clue.text: No doubt he boasts more than one pair of hands

definitions.text: No doubt he boasts more than one pair of hands

parts.words: No doubt he boasts more than one pair of hands
parts.note: hands are workers, and a boss has many on the payroll

explanation.surface: A many-armed boaster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hands' means hired workers, so the boss has many of them.
explanation.definitionFit: A boss hires staff, so he has many hired hands working for him.
